title: Esau runs
hook: twenty years after being cheated, Esau runs to embrace Jacob (Genesis 33:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in a room in Egypt. Your line was he wept aloud. Did your shoulders drop, even one degree? Today, another pair of brothers in Genesis, and this time, the wronged one runs. Day nine hundred forty-four.

Dust on the horizon. Jacob looks up, and there is his brother Esau, and with him, the text says, four hundred men. The last time they were together, Jacob dressed up as Esau, fooled their blind father, and walked off with the blessing meant for his brother. Esau said in his heart that he would kill him. Jacob ran, and stayed away a long time; in his own words to his father-in-law, twenty years. Now he's coming home, and he's limping from a night of wrestling by the river. He has sent gifts ahead, flocks and herds, wave after wave. He has split his camp in two, in case one half is attacked. And now he walks out in front of them all.
screen: `DUST ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE STOLEN BLESSING.` → `JACOB WALKS OUT IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob bows. The King James says he "bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother." It's the posture of a man expecting the worst and hoping to soften it. Second, Esau runs. And here is the whole surprise, in one verse: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech first. No terms. No demand for an apology. The text never says what changed in Esau over those years. It only shows us his feet. Third, the gifts. Jacob keeps pressing the flocks on him, and Esau waves them off: "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob won't let it go. "Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee." Some readers notice the word. Blessing. The very thing he stole years before, and here he is, trying to hand a blessing back. Fourth, a face. Jacob says something strange to his brother: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God." The night before, he had wrestled until dawn and named the place for seeing God face to face. Now he says the same thing about his brother's face. Readers have heard different things in that line. One reading: a face that should have been angry and is kind instead is about as close to the divine as it gets. The story doesn't tie a bow on it. The brothers part ways again soon after. But for one morning, the wronged one ran.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES TO THE GROUND.` · `ESAU RAN TO MEET HIM.` · `I HAVE ENOUGH, MY BROTHER.` · `AS THOUGH THE FACE OF GOD.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you've drifted from: a brother or sister, a cousin, an old friend, someone where things went quiet after a hurt, on either side. You don't have to fix the whole story. Ask only this: what is one step toward them? A message that just says hello. A photo you could send. A question about their kids. Choose the smallest step that's still a step. Hold it, and let your feet feel the floor, as if they're ready to move. If you pray, you can hold this person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Esau runs. Years after Jacob cheated him of the blessing, Esau runs to meet his brother, embraces him, and they weep. Today's word.
Your line: he ran to meet him. Today, take the one small step you chose toward that person. Not the whole way. One step. Day nine hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read the meeting of Jacob and Esau in the yearly cycle of Torah readings in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis; it is taught as a story of brothers reconciled after a deep wrong.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old family quarrel, patched up.
what it means: the brother who was cheated runs to the one who cheated him, with no terms.
what a scholar hears: Jacob offers his 'blessing' (Genesis 33:11), the word for what he once stole, and calls Esau's face like the face of God (33:10), echoing the wrestling night at Peniel.

notes: 'Twenty years' is Jacob's own figure to Laban (Genesis 31:38, 31:41); the script attributes it to him. 'Four hundred men' is Genesis 32:6 and 33:1; 'seven times' is 33:3.
Genesis 33:10 in KJV reads 'for therefore I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me'; the script quotes the middle phrase only.
The connection between 'blessing' in 33:11 and the stolen blessing of Genesis 27 is attributed to 'some readers'; a reviewer should confirm the Hebrew word (berakhah) is the same in both places.
The echo of Peniel (32:30) in 33:10 is offered as 'one reading'.

Original-language entry: וַיָּרָץ as the first word of Genesis 33:4. Confirm vocalization and pronunciation. The dotted word over 'kissed him' in the Masoretic text is deliberately not mentioned (manuscript claim).
'They part ways again soon after' summarizes Genesis 33:12–17.

Editor pass: 'Esau swore he'd kill him' corrected to Genesis 27:41's wording (he said in his heart he would slay his brother); review line changed from 'the one who was wronged moves first', since Joseph, the wronged brother of day 943, also moved first.
